questions.prompt: What condition on one-sided limits makes \(\lim_{x\to a}f(x)\) exist?
questions.answer:
The two-sided limit exists exactly when both one-sided limits exist and are equal:
\[\lim_{x\to a^-}f(x)=\lim_{x\to a^+}f(x).\]
Their common value is the two-sided limit.

\[\lim_{x\to2}f(x)=5.\]

As \(x\to2^-\), the quantity \(x-2\) is negative and approaches \(0\).

questions.prompt: For \(f(x)=\begin{cases}x+1,&x<0\2x+1,&x>0\end{cases}\), find \(\lim_{x\to0^-}f(x)\), \(\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)\), and the two-sided limit.
questions.answer:
From the left, use \(x+1\):
\[\lim_{x\to0^-}f(x)=0+1=1.\]
From the right, use \(2x+1\):
\[\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)=2(0)+1=1.\]
Since both one-sided limits are equal,
\[\lim_{x\to0}f(x)=1.\]

The left-hand limit is
\[\lim_{x\to3^-}f(x)=1.\]
The right-hand limit is
\[\lim_{x\to3^+}f(x)=4.\]
Since \(1\ne4\), the two-sided limit does not exist.

questions.prompt: Evaluate \(\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{7x-1}{x^2+4}\) and interpret the horizontal behavior.
questions.answer:
Divide by \(x^2\):
\[\frac{7x-1}{x^2+4}=\frac{7/x-1/x^2}{1+4/x^2}.\]
All reciprocal terms in the numerator approach \(0\), while the denominator approaches \(1\).
The limit is \(0\), so the graph approaches the horizontal asymptote \(y=0\) to the right.

On both sides of \(1\), \((x-1)^2\) is positive and approaches \(0\).
Thus \(\frac2{(x-1)^2}\) grows without bound from both directions:
\[\lim_{x\to1^+}\frac2{(x-1)^2}=+\infty,\qquad \lim_{x\to1^-}\frac2{(x-1)^2}=+\infty.\]

If \(x\to0^+\), then \(x^3\) is positive and approaches \(0\), so
\[\lim_{x\to0^+}\frac1{x^3}=+\infty.\]
If \(x\to0^-\), then \(x^3\) is negative and approaches \(0\), so
\[\lim_{x\to0^-}\frac1{x^3}=-\infty.\]

questions.prompt: For \(\frac{x^2+1}{x-4}\), classify the behavior as \(x\to4^+\) and \(x\to4^-\).
questions.answer:
Near \(x=4\), the numerator \(x^2+1\) is positive and close to \(17\).
The denominator \(x-4\) approaches \(0\). From the right it is positive, so the quotient approaches \(+\infty\). From the left it is negative, so the quotient approaches \(-\infty\).
Thus
\[\lim_{x\to4^+}\frac{x^2+1}{x-4}=+\infty,\qquad \lim_{x\to4^-}\frac{x^2+1}{x-4}=-\infty.\]

questions.prompt: A student says \(\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{3x^2+10}{x}=3\) by comparing coefficients. Diagnose the error and find the correct behavior.
questions.answer:
The degrees are not equal. Divide by \(x\):
\[\frac{3x^2+10}{x}=3x+\frac{10}{x}.\]
As \(x\to\infty\), \(3x\to\infty\) and \(10/x\to0\).
So the expression grows without bound:
\[\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{3x^2+10}{x}=+\infty.\]

questions.prompt: Construct a simple piecewise function whose left-hand limit at \(0\) is \(-1\) and right-hand limit at \(0\) is \(1\), and state the two-sided limit.
questions.answer:
One example is
\[f(x)=\begin{cases}-1,&x<0\1,&x>0.\end{cases}\]
Then
\[\lim_{x\to0^-}f(x)=-1,\qquad \lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)=1.\]
Since the one-sided limits are different, \(\lim_{x\to0}f(x)\) does not exist.

questions.prompt: Explain why \(\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=+\infty\) is not a finite limit, even though it describes limiting behavior.
questions.answer:
A finite limit \(L\) means \(f(x)\) gets arbitrarily close to a real number \(L\).
The statement \(\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=+\infty\) means \(f(x)\) eventually exceeds every positive bound as \(x\) approaches \(a\).
So it describes unbounded behavior, not approach to a real number. It is an infinite limit, not a finite limit.
